summary: Describes private SIP extensions that let a network of trusted SIP servers assert the service of authenticated users. They apply only within an administrative domain with prior agreed policies. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Inside a trusted group of phone servers, they can tell one another what kind of service a caller is using. This describes the extra header for that.

questions: how do sip proxies determine service
subtitle: Two headers that let trusted SIP servers tell each other what service a call is using.

tldr.problem: When a SIP call arrives at a proxy, the proxy may need to understand what service the user is requesting in order to know how to route or handle it. This can require expensive analysis of the SIP message and SDP.
tldr.mechanism: Two new SIP headers identify the service within a trusted domain. The P-Asserted-Service header carries a service identifier from one trusted proxy to another. The P-Preferred-Service header lets the calling user express a preference about which service the trusted network should use.
tldr.outcome: Proxies can cache the results of expensive service analysis, and trusted proxies downstream do not have to repeat it. It is an Informational RFC limited to use within administrative trust domains.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: Trust domains only; not for public Internet use

today: RFC 6050 is an Informational RFC published in November 2010. It remains the specification for service identification within trusted SIP domains, and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 6050 defines private extensions to the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) that allow a network of trusted SIP servers to identify and assert the service that a user is requesting. A trusted SIP server can examine a call, determine what service the caller is using (for example, a video call, a push-to-talk session, or an IP TV broadcast), and pass that information to other trusted servers by adding a special header to the SIP message.

The mechanism is designed only for use within a single administrative domain where all servers trust each other. It does not offer a way for users to communicate service information across different networks or on the public Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: Inside a trusted phone network, servers can add a label to a call that says what kind of service it is. This label only works between servers that trust each other.

sections.title: Why Service Identification Matters
sections.content:
A proxy server that receives a SIP INVITE request contains all the information needed to figure out what service is being requested: the request type, the SDP session description, and other headers. However, calculating the service may require examining the SDP and checking the user's entitlements, which can be computationally intensive. For example, an INVITE with video SDP to a video-on-demand address should be identified as an IPTV session; an INVITE with push-to-talk routes should be marked as PoC (Push-to-Talk over Cellular).

By allowing one trusted proxy to perform this analysis once, determine the service, and assert it in a header, downstream trusted proxies and trusted user agents can use the asserted service without redoing the analysis.
sections.plainLanguage: Working out what kind of service a call is takes effort. If one trusted server figures it out and tells the others, the others save work.

sections.title: The Service Headers
sections.content:
RFC 6050 defines two new SIP headers:

P-Asserted-Service carries the service identifier that a trusted proxy has determined. Proxies within a trust domain can add this header after authenticating the user and verifying they are entitled to the service. When a proxy forwards the request to another trusted proxy, it includes the P-Asserted-Service header. When it forwards to an untrusted node or outside the trust domain, it MUST remove the header.

P-Preferred-Service allows the calling user agent to hint at the preferred service it wants. The proxy MAY use this hint to prioritize its service identification logic, but it MUST NOT rely on it alone. The proxy must verify the hint against the capabilities (like SDP) in the request.

Service identifiers use a Uniform Resource Name (URN) format. An example is urn:urn-7:3gpp-service.exampletelephony.version1. The namespace identifier urn-7 is registered with IANA, and organizations like 3GPP can register their top-level service identifiers and define subservices.
sections.plainLanguage: One header says which service the network determined the call is using. The other lets the phone suggest what service it wants. Both use special names that look like web addresses.

sections.title: Service Identifier Structure
sections.content:
Service identifiers follow a hierarchical structure defined in RFC 6050. A service identifier consists of labels separated by periods, like domain names. The leftmost label is the top-level service identifier (for example, 3gpp-service), and labels to the right are subservices.

Labels are case-insensitive and must be lowercase. Allowed characters are alphanumerics and hyphens, the same as domain names. The structure supports the notion that a partial service identifier is still valid; for example, if 3gpp-service.example.version1 is a service, then 3gpp-service.example and 3gpp-service are also valid, referring to more generic services.

IANA maintains a registry of top-level service identifiers. Only IANA action can add a new top-level identifier. The organizations that register a top-level identifier manage their own subservice registries. For example, 3GPP registered 3gpp-service and 3gpp-application and can define subservices under each.
sections.plainLanguage: Service names are like web addresses, with periods separating the parts. You can drop the rightmost parts and still have a valid name that means a more general service.

sections.title: Usage in Trusted Domains
sections.content:
A trust domain, as defined in RFC 3324, is a set of SIP nodes that are explicitly trusted by all users and systems in that domain. All nodes must agree on service definitions.

When a proxy receives a request from an untrusted source, it MAY authenticate the user and determine the service based on the request content (SDP, request type, etc.). If it does, it MUST insert a P-Asserted-Service header containing the service it determined. When forwarding to a trusted peer, it keeps the header. When forwarding outside the trust domain, it MUST remove it.

When a proxy receives a request from a trusted peer that already carries a P-Asserted-Service header, it can trust that header and use it directly. If there is no header, the proxy MAY add one based on its own analysis.

User agent clients in the trust domain may include a P-Preferred-Service header to suggest a service. Servers use this as a hint, but they MUST verify the actual service based on the call's capabilities before inserting P-Asserted-Service.
sections.plainLanguage: Servers in a trusted network authenticate calls, figure out the service, and pass that information on to the next server in the network. They drop the information before sending outside the network.

sections.title: Security and Trust
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that this mechanism relies entirely on the trust domain boundary. Service information is protected by transitive trust: if a trusted proxy asserts a service, downstream proxies trust it. The information is no more reliable than the weakest link in the chain of trust.

RFC 6050 stresses that these extensions do NOT provide cryptographic assurance of the service identifier. A forged or replayed header can cause problems within an untrusted network. These extensions are only safe when all nodes in the trust domain are administratively controlled and meet the requirements of RFC 3324.

The extensions assume a closed, homogeneous network. An end user cannot assert their own service on the public Internet using these mechanisms; the RFC explicitly rejects declarative service identification (where a user claims a service). Only derived service identification, where a trusted network determines the service based on the request itself, is supported.
sections.plainLanguage: This only works when all servers trust each other completely. On the public Internet, anyone could lie about the service, so this mechanism is only for private networks.
